title: United States v. Arthrex, Inc. (2021)
summary: Administrative patent judges could not make final unreviewable executive decisions under their inferior-officer appointments; allowing Director review supplied the tailored remedy.

sections.Parties: Arthrex, a medical-device patent owner, challenged the authority of administrative patent judges who ruled its patent invalid. Smith & Nephew and ArthroCare sought inter partes review, and the United States intervened to defend the appointment scheme.
sections.Material Facts: Arthrex patented a surgical device for reattaching soft tissue to bone without a knot. A three-judge Patent Trial and Appeal Board panel found that a prior application anticipated the claimed invention. The Secretary of Commerce appointed the administrative patent judges. The Senate-confirmed PTO Director supervised institutional matters, selected panels, and controlled initiation of review, but a statutory provision reserved rehearing to the Board, preventing the Director from independently reviewing its final patentability decisions. Judges also had removal protections.
sections.Procedural History: The Federal Circuit agreed that the judges exercised impermissible principal-officer authority, severed their removal protections, vacated the Board decision, and required a new panel. The Supreme Court vacated that appellate judgment and remanded for the Acting Director to decide whether to rehear the petition. It did not require a new panel or invalidate inter partes review as a whole.
sections.Issue: Was final decisionmaking insulated from principal-officer review compatible with appointment by a department head as inferior officers, and what relief should follow?
sections.Holding: It was incompatible in this adjudicative setting. Section 6(c) could not be enforced to prevent the Director from reviewing final Board decisions and issuing his own decision. The Director’s discretion to review, without reviewing every case, supplied the necessary supervision.
sections.Reasoning: The merits majority applied Edmond’s direction-and-supervision approach. Control over pay, panels, and prospective policy did not give a politically accountable principal officer authority over the actual final patent decision. Panel manipulation would obscure responsibility, and judicial review by the Federal Circuit could not supply supervision within the Executive Branch. The Court declined to announce an exclusive test for every officer or for nonadjudicative functions. On remedy, Director review fit the statutory structure more closely than removing tenure protections and addressed the precise constitutional defect. Roberts’s Parts I and II commanded a majority; the remedial result drew a different coalition. Gorsuch agreed on the violation but would set aside the Board decision instead of reshaping the review scheme. Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan disagreed on the violation but supported the tailored remedy given the majority’s premise. Thomas emphasized the judges’ actual subordination and disputed making final review dispositive. Their positions must remain distinct.

topics.lrs-s-inferior-officer: Final unreviewable executive adjudication exceeded the authority compatible with these inferior-officer appointments.
topics.lrs-s-severability: The Court remedied the defect by permitting Director review while preserving the broader adjudicatory scheme.
topics.lrs-s-accountability: Review by a principal officer made responsibility for final agency decisions visible.
topics.lrs-s-appointments-clause: Arthrex turns on whether APJs appointed by the Secretary of Commerce exercised authority reserved to presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed principal officers.
topics.lrs-s-article-ii-appointments: The decision applies the text of Article II, § 2, cl. 2 distinguishing principal from inferior officers.
